sections.overview: The capybara is the largest living rodent, native to much of South America and strongly associated with wetlands and other water-rich landscapes.
sections.identification: Its large barrel-shaped body, blunt muzzle, short legs and sparse coat distinguish it from smaller caviid rodents.
sections.habitat: It uses wetlands, riverbanks and seasonally flooded grasslands, relying on nearby water for cooling and escape from danger.
sections.diet: It grazes mainly on grasses and aquatic plants, with bark and fruit taken less often.
sections.behavior: When alarmed, it gives a bark-like call and escapes into the water, where it swims and dives well.
sections.reproduction: Mating usually takes place in water, and females give birth to litters whose young can join the group soon after birth.
sections.ecology: The lesser capybara Hydrochoerus isthmius is a close relative in the same genus, but some mammal taxonomies still treat its species status cautiously or include it within H. hydrochaeris.
sections.conservation: The IUCN’s 2016 global assessment lists H. hydrochaeris as Least Concern with a stable trend, while noting local pressures such as hunting.
